Here are verse-by-verse notes on 1 Chronicles 22, drawing from the approved sources:

---

## 1 Chronicles 22 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### v. 1 — David Declares the Temple Site

**Traditional Reading:** David, likely by divine impulse, publicly identifies the threshing floor of Ornan (Araunah) the Jebusite — which he had just purchased and where God answered by fire — as the divinely chosen location for both the temple ("the house of the LORD God") and the altar of burnt offering. This fulfills Deuteronomy 12:5, where God promised to choose a place for His name to dwell. The site is later identified in 2 Chronicles 3:1 as Mount Moriah, where the Angel of the LORD had appeared to David (a Christophany, as some interpreters note). This verse is the narrative goal of the census-and-plague story: the Chronicler shows *how* the temple site was determined.

- David "said" — possibly to himself or to those around him, under divine impulse. Gill notes the Hebrew idiom allows "This is the place where the house shall be." God had accepted the sacrifice (1 Chron. 21:26), judgment had passed, and prayer was answered; David could now truthfully declare the site. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-22-commentary)
- Gill adds that the threshing floor being Jebusite (Gentile) land "might prefigure the church of God to be built up among the Gentiles." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/22.htm)
- Ellicott renders: "This is a house of Jehovah, the (true) God, and this (is) an altar of burnt offering for Israel," comparing it to Genesis 28:17 ("this is the house of God"). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-22.html)
- Precept Austin notes Warren Wiersbe's observation: it is remarkable that the temple was built on property purchased because of David's sin (the census), and built by Solomon (a son of Bathsheba). "Only God can take a man's two greatest sins and build a temple out of them." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-22-commentary)

---

### v. 2 — Foreigners Drafted as Stonecutters

**Traditional Reading:** David conscripted the "foreigners" (gērîm — resident aliens, descendants of the Canaanites living under Israelite dominion) to quarry and dress stones for the future temple. This follows the principle that conquered peoples were liable to forced labour (1 Kings 9:20–21; 2 Chron. 8:7–8). Chapters 22–29 are unique to Chronicles, having no parallel in Samuel or Kings.

- Ellicott identifies the "strangers" as the Canaanite population "who lived on sufferance under the Israelite dominion." Solomon later found them by census to number 153,600 (2 Chron. 2:17–18). The Hebrew verb for "gather" (kânas) is a late term, characteristic of the Chronicler's style. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-22.html)
- Gill notes these were "proselytes of the gate" (those who accepted the seven Noachide laws) and that their employment "denotes that the Gentiles would be concerned in building the spiritual house and church of God." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/22.htm)
- Enduring Word adds: "Only Jews built the tabernacle, but the temple is not built without the aid of the Gentile Tyrians. They, together with us, make up the Church of God" (Trapp). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-22/)
- Precept Austin cites Utley noting three groups of labourers: skilled Phoenician workers, forced labour from conquered nations, and forced labour from Israelite tribes (1 Kings 5:13–16). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-22-commentary)

---

### v. 3 — Iron and Bronze in Abundance

**Traditional Reading:** David stockpiled iron (for nails, door fittings, and clamps) and bronze "beyond measure." Iron technology had been a Philistine monopoly (1 Sam. 13:19–22), so David's accumulation of iron signals the Philistines' subjugation (1 Chron. 18:1). Bronze was used extensively in ornamental and structural work.

- Ellicott notes "without weight" is "a natural hyperbole. The actual amounts would, of course, be known to the royal treasurers." He compares the Assyrian phrases *la niba, la mani* ("without number, without measure") used of spoils. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-22.html)
- Precept Austin: "Iron technology was unique to the Philistines… the fact that David had gathered much iron demonstrates the subjugation of the Philistines." The IVP Bible Background Commentary notes iron was still considered decorative in this period (Iron I). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-22-commentary)

---

### v. 4 — Cedar Logs from the Phoenicians

**Traditional Reading:** The Sidonians and Tyrians (Phoenicians) supplied vast quantities of cedar from Lebanon — legendary for its excellent timber — in ordinary commerce, bartering for Israel's grain, wine, and oil. Later, Hiram of Tyre entered a formal contract with Solomon (1 Kings 5:8–11).

- Ellicott calls the phrase "beams or logs of cedars without number" a "rhetorical exaggeration" like v. 3. The cedar came "in the way of ordinary commerce," not yet by treaty. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-22.html)
- Enduring Word: "This means David (and Solomon after him) wanted to build the temple out of the best materials possible." Gentile wood and Gentile labour point to a temple "not only for Israel." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-22/)

---

### v. 5 — Solomon's Youth and the Temple's Magnificence

**Traditional Reading:** David explains his motivation for making "lavish preparations": Solomon is "young and inexperienced" (the Hebrew *na'ar* is a flexible term — it can mean anything from a newborn to a man in his prime; Solomon himself used it after accession in 1 Kings 3:7), and the temple must be "exceedingly magnificent, famous and glorious throughout all lands." David's advanced age and approaching death quickened his diligence.

- Matthew Henry: "The consideration of his age and growing infirmities, which showed him his death approaching, quickened him… What our hands find to do for God, and our souls, and our generation, let us do it with all our might before our death, because, after death, there is no device nor working." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_chronicles/22.htm)
- Enduring Word: "We can almost picture the old David and the young Solomon pouring over the plans and ideas for the temple together with excitement. David… had the right vision for what the temple should be… and he passed that vision on to his son." The commentator (Guzik) calls this "a picture of a man who through stress and storm had found his way into the quiet calm assurance of his place in the divine economy" (quoting G. Campbell Morgan). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-22/)
- Ellicott notes the Hebrew for "exceeding magnifical" is literally "to make great exceedingly, unto height, upwards" — an adverbial phrase characteristic of Chronicles. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-22.html)

---

### vv. 6–10 — David's Charge to Solomon: Why David Cannot Build

**Traditional Reading:** David summons Solomon and delivers a sacred charge (not a suggestion). He recounts: (a) it was in his heart to build; (b) God forbade him because he "shed much blood and waged great wars"; (c) God promised a "man of rest" — Solomon (whose name means "peaceful") — who would build instead; and (d) God pledged to be a Father to Solomon and establish his throne "forever." This explanation of the bloodshed prohibition is unique to Chronicles; 2 Samuel 7 and 1 Kings 5 only mention David's wars leaving no leisure.

- The bloodshed reason: Enduring Word stresses it was not that David's wars were sinful, but that "God wanted His house built from the context of peace and rest and victory… after and from the victory, not from the midst of struggle." Matthew Poole adds it was "principally for mystical signification, to teach us that the church… should be built by Christ, the Prince of peace… and that it should be gathered and built up, not by might or power, or by force of arms, but by God's Spirit." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-22/)
- Gill: "An intimation this, that the church of God… was to be built by Christ, the Prince of peace, and to be supported and maintained not by force of arms, and by spilling of blood, as the religion of Mahomet, but by the preaching of the Gospel of peace." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/22.htm)
- Ellicott observes that the "word of the Lord" here only partially corresponds to Nathan's oracle in 1 Chron. 17:4–14 — there, David was promised success in war *without* any hint warfare would disqualify him. He suggests the verse "may express the interpretation which David's own conscience put upon the oracle." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-22.html)

**v. 10 — The Davidic Covenant and "Forever":** This verse echoes the Nathan oracle (1 Chron. 17; 2 Sam. 7) and the language of sonship applied to the Davidic king. Hebrews 1:5 applies "I will be his Father, and he shall be My son" to Christ. Gill notes this "will have its fulfilment in Christ, his antitype, in the utmost sense of the expression, whose kingdom is an everlasting kingdom." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/22.htm)

---

### vv. 11–13 — David's Blessing and Warning

**Traditional Reading:** David prays for the LORD's presence with Solomon, for wisdom and understanding, and for success in building — "as He said you would." But he immediately grounds success in a condition: "if you carefully follow the statutes and ordinances." He then exhorts, "Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or discouraged" — echoing Joshua 1:6–9 and Deuteronomy 31:6–8. The presence of God, obedience to the law, and courage are inseparably linked.

- Enduring Word: "David knew that Solomon could not be strong or courageous without obedient fellowship with God. In this place of obedient fellowship, Solomon would prosper in all that he did." The promise of the throne's endurance was conditional on obedience (1 Kings 2:1–4). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-22/)
- Ellicott: "The verse makes it quite clear that obedience was an indispensable condition to the full realisation of the promise. Yet the word of the Lord does not return unto Him void; and if the earthly dynasty of David came to an end through disobedience, in due time was born an heir of David and Solomon, who is at this day the Lord of a spiritual dominion which will endure throughout the ages." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-22.html)
- Matthew Henry: "He must not think by building the temple to purchase a dispensation to sin; no, on the contrary, his doing that would not be accepted, nor accounted of, if he did not take heed to fulfil the statutes… Though he was to be king of Israel, he must always remember that he was a subject to the God of Israel." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_chronicles/22.htm)
- Precept Austin notes that David's charge begins (v. 11) and ends (v. 16) with the prayer "the LORD be with you" — forming an inclusio that frames the whole charge. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-22-commentary)

---

### vv. 14–16 — David's Material Preparations and Charge to Begin

**Traditional Reading:** David itemises his preparations: 100,000 talents of gold, 1,000,000 talents of silver, bronze and iron beyond weight, timber, stone, and craftsmen beyond number. He then urges Solomon: "Now begin the work, and may the LORD be with you." The quantities are enormous and debated.

- **The Numbers:** Ellicott notes that even at conservative valuations (£6,000 per gold talent, £400 per silver talent), the sums are "incredibly large." He argues these are round numbers in thousands, "used in rhetorical fashion to suggest amounts of extraordinary magnitude" — like the Assyrian use of "without number." "Doubtless, a modern historian would not handle exact numbers in this liberal manner; but we are not, therefore, bound to construe these vivid Oriental exaggerations according to the strict letter rather than the spirit." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-22.html)
- Gill surveys various scholarly estimates and notes Josephus reduced the figures to 10,000 talents of gold and 100,000 of silver, while Prideaux computed the Mosaic-talent value at over 800 million pounds sterling. Gill suggests the Hebrew *kikkar* may signify "a cake or mass of gold of an uncertain value" rather than a full talent. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/22.htm)

- **"You may add to them":** David models generosity but also invites Solomon to contribute his own. Enduring Word, quoting Spurgeon: "Cannot I put my hand on some young man's shoulder, and say to him, 'Thou mayest add thereto; thou hast a good voice; thou hast an active brain; begin to speak for God'?" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-22/)
- **David's Hidden Labour:** Enduring Word lists what David did that typically goes to Solomon's credit: gathered materials, prepared them, won peace with nations, purchased the site, established the plans, and organized the administration. "Yet no one calls it 'David's temple'… It doesn't seem to have bothered David, because he was a man after God's heart." Spurgeon: "God buries the workman, but the devil himself cannot bury the work. The work is everlasting, though the workmen die." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-22/)
- **Christological typology:** Enduring Word notes Jesus, the greater Son of David, is also building a temple (Eph. 2:19–22). "He could only do this after security and treasure were won, but the greater Son of David made this peace and plundered the enemy Himself at the cross." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-22/)

---

### vv. 17–19 — David's Command to Israel's Leaders

**Traditional Reading:** David commands "all the leaders of Israel" to help Solomon. He grounds his appeal in what God has already done: the LORD is with them, He has given rest on every side, and the land is subdued. Therefore they should "set your heart and soul to seek the LORD your God" — and the way to do that, practically, is to arise and build the sanctuary. The ultimate goal is to bring the ark of the covenant and the holy vessels into a permanent home.

- Enduring Word: "David knew that one leader – even a great leader – was not enough to get a great work done. When God calls a leader He also calls other leaders… to help." The command to "seek the LORD" is given "in the context of work, not the context of leisurely repose before God. David knew that it was possible to keep one's heart set on seeking God even in the midst of doing a great work." Quoting Selman: "'Seeking' is an act of obedience rather than a search for guidance." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-22/)
- Ellicott: "Building the Lord a fair and noble sanctuary was equivalent to seeking His favour. Professions cost nothing, and they were not to serve the Lord 'without cost' (1 Chron. 21:24)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-22.html)
- Matthew Henry: "Where God gives rest he expects work." David's appeal is to what God has *already* done for them, making gratitude the motive for service. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_chronicles/22.htm)
- Adam Clarke (cited by Enduring Word) adds a somber note on Solomon: "Thus Solomon came to the Jewish throne with every possible advantage. Had he made a proper use of his state and of his talents, he would have been the greatest as well as the wisest of sovereigns. But alas! How soon did this pure gold become dim!" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-22/)

---

## Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

On this particular chapter, most of the approved Protestant sources converge on the same basic reading. Differences tend to be matters of emphasis rather than contradictory interpretation. However, the following distinctions can be noted:

**1. The conditional nature of the promise (vv. 10, 13):**

- **Reformed/Covenant Theology** (seen in Ellicott and Matthew Henry) emphasises that while the earthly Davidic dynasty fell through disobedience, the unconditional aspect of the covenant is fulfilled in Christ alone — the "forever" promise finds its ultimate meaning in Him. The conditionality applied to Solomon's line but not to the ultimate Son of David. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-22.html)
- **Enduring Word** (broadly evangelical/Pentecostal-leaning) stresses the promise that "as long as David's sons walked in obedience, they would keep the throne" — emphasising the genuine conditionality and the practical need for faithfulness. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-22/)

**2. The Gentiles in temple-building (vv. 2, 4):**

- **Gill / older Reformed Baptist:** Reads the foreigners' involvement as typological, prefiguring Gentile inclusion in the Church. "This is another thing prefiguring the help of the Gentiles in building up the church of Christ in Gospel times." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/22.htm)
- **Enduring Word / Pentecostal-charismatic:** Similarly sees Gentile involvement as pointing to the universal Church: "This was a temple to the God of Israel, but it was not only for Israel." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-22/)

**3. The enormous quantities of gold and silver (v. 14):**

- **Ellicott / modern critical approach:** Treats the figures as "rhetorical" and "vivid Oriental exaggerations," not meant to be taken literally. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-22.html)
- **Gill / traditional approach:** Engages seriously with possible valuations, considers Josephus's reduced figures, and allows that the Hebrew *kikkar* may denote a smaller unit. Does not dismiss the numbers as mere rhetoric. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/22.htm)
- **Enduring Word:** Acknowledges that "some Bible commentators believe this large number is accurate and some feel it is a scribal error," but concludes: "Even allowing for possible scribal error, David clearly amassed significant resources." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-22/)

---

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (Ellicott, representing a critical approach):**

- Ellicott suggests David's speeches in this chapter are "an ideal composition, put into the king's mouth by the unknown author whose work the chronicler follows: or rather, perhaps, by the chronicler himself, whose style is evident throughout." He compares them to the addresses in 1 Chronicles 28. The narrative is theologically crafted, not a transcript. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-22.html)
- He also notes that Gramberg and other critics alleged "the whole episode about David's preparations is a fiction of the chronist's" because Samuel and Kings are silent. Ellicott finds this argument lacking in "the historical faculty." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-22.html)

**Catholic and Orthodox Readings:**

- A thorough search of newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org returned no specific verse-by-verse treatment of 1 Chronicles 22 from those sites. The Catholic tradition (represented by the Vulgate's *Pacificus* for Solomon) and Orthodox typological reading of the temple would likely emphasise the temple as type of the Church and of the Theotokos (the "house" of God), but this was not directly retrievable from the approved sources within the search limits.

**Debated Modern Teaching:**

- No prosperity-gospel, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace teaching specific to this chapter surfaced from the approved source list. Prosperity teachers might appeal to vv. 13–14 to link obedience with material prosperity and to David's massive wealth as evidence of divine blessing, but no such teaching from an approved site was found.

---

*Sources used: Enduring Word (David Guzik), Precept Austin, Gill's Exposition, Ellicott's Commentary for English Readers, Matthew Henry's Commentary (Concise), Bridgeway Bible Commentary, and linked cross-references.*
